# Calculation of gas energy ratio for gaseous fuels (LPG and NG/biomethane)

1. Measurement of the mass of gaseous fuel consumed during the Type 1 test cycle

Measurement of the mass of gas consumed during the cycle shall be done by a fuel weighing system capable of measuring the weight of the storage container during the test in accordance with the following:

(a) An accuracy of $\pm \nobreakspace 2 \nobreakspace$ per cent of the difference between the readings at the beginning and at the end of the test or better.   
(b) Precautions shall be taken to avoid measurement errors. Such precautions shall at least include the careful installation of the device in accordance with the instrument manufacturer's recommendations and to good engineering practice.   
(c) Other measurement methods are permitted if an equivalent accuracy can be demonstrated.

2. Calculation of the gas energy ratio

The fuel consumption value shall be calculated from the emissions of hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide determined from the measurement results assuming that only the gaseous fuel is burned during the test.

The gas ratio of the energy consumed in the cycle shall be determined using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { G } _ { \mathrm { g a s } } = \left( \frac { \mathrm { M } _ { \mathrm { g a s } } \times \mathrm { c f } \times 1 0 ^ { 4 } } { \mathrm { F C } _ { \mathrm { n o r m } } \times \mathrm { d i s t } \times \rho } \right)
$$

where:

Ggas is the gas energy ratio, per cent;   
$\mathrm { M _ { g a s } }$ is the mass of the gaseous fuel consumed during the cycle, kg;   
FCnorm is the fuel consumption ( $1 / 1 0 0 \mathrm { k m }$ for LPG, $\mathrm { m } ^ { 3 } / 1 0 0 \mathrm { k m }$ for NG/biomethane) calculated in accordance with paragraphs 6.6. and 6.7. of Sub-Annex 7;   
dist is the distance recorded during the cycle, km;   
ρ is the gas density: $\mathrm { ~ \ p ~ = ~ } 0 , 6 5 4 \mathrm { k g / m } ^ { 3 }$ for NG/Biomethane; $\rho = 0 , 5 3 8 { \mathrm { k g } } / 1$ itre for LPG;   
cf is the correction factor, assuming the following values: $\operatorname { c f } = 1$ in the case of LPG or G20 reference fuel; cf $\cdot = 0 { , } 7 8$ in the case of G25 reference fuel.

Ambient Temperature Correction Test for the determination of $\mathbf { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions under representative regional temperature conditions

1. Introduction

This Sub-Annex describes the supplemental Ambient Temperature Correction Test (ATCT) procedure to determine the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions under representative regional temperature conditions.

1.1. The $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions of ICE vehicles, NOVC-HEVs and the charge sustaining value of OVC-HEVs shall be corrected in accordance with the requirements of this Sub-Annex. No correction is required for the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ value of the charge depleting test. No correction is required for an Electric Range.

2. Ambient Temperature Correction Test (ATCT) Family

2.1. Only vehicles which are identical with respect to all the following characteristics are permitted to be part of the same ATCT Family:

(a) Powertrain architecture (i.e. internal combustion, hybrid, fuel cell, or electric);   
(b) Combustion process (i.e. two stroke or four stroke);   
(c) Number and arrangement of cylinders;   
(d) Method of engine combustion (i.e. indirect or direct injection);   
(e) Type of cooling system (i.e. air, water, or oil);   
(f) Method of aspiration (i.e. naturally aspirated, or charged);   
(g) Fuel for which the engine is designed (i.e. petrol, diesel, NG, LPG, etc.);   
(h) Catalytic converter (i.e. three-way catalyst, lean $\mathrm { N O } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ trap, SCR, lean $\mathrm { N O } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ catalyst or other(s));   
(i) Whether or not a particulate trap is installed; and   
(j) Exhaust gas recirculation (with or without, cooled or non-cooled).

In addition the vehicles shall be similar with respect to the following characteristics:

(k) The vehicles shall have a variation in engine cylinder capacity of no more than $30 \%$ of the vehicle with the lowest capacity; and

(l) Engine compartment insulation shall be of a similar type regarding material, amount and location of the insulation. Manufacturers shall provide evidence (e.g. by CAD drawings) to the approval authority that for all vehicles in the family, the volume and weight of the insulation material which will be installed is greater than $90 \%$ of that of the ATCT measured reference vehicle.

Difference in insulation material and location may also be accepted to be part of a single ATCT family under the condition that the test vehicle can be demonstrated as being the worst case with regards to engine compartment insulation.

2.1.1. If active heat storage devices are installed, only vehicles that meet the following requirements shall be considered to be part of the same ATCT Family:

(i) the heat capacity, defined by the enthalpy stored in the system, is within a range of 0 to $10 \%$ above the enthalpy of the test vehicle; and   
(ii) the OEM can provide evidence to the technical service that the time for heat release at engine start within a family is within a range of 0 to $10 \%$ below the time for the heat release of the test vehicle.

2.1.2. Only vehicles that meet the criteria set out in paragraph 3.9.4. of this Sub-Annex 6a shall be considered to be part of the same ATCT Family.

3. ATCT Procedure

The Type 1 test specified in Sub-Annex 6 shall be carried out with the exception of the requirements specified in paragraphs 3.1. to 3.9. of this Sub-Annex 6a. That requires also a new calculation and application of gearshift points in accordance with Sub-Annex 2 taking into account the different road load as specified in paragraph 3.4. of this Sub-Annex 6a.

3.1. Ambient conditions for ATCT

3.1.1. The temperature $( \mathrm { T _ { r e g } } )$ at which the vehicle should be soaked and tested for the ATCT shall be $1 4 ~ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .

3.1.2. The minimum soaking time (tsoak_ATCT) for the ATCT shall be 9 hours.

3.2. Test cell and soak area

3.2.1. Test cell

3.2.1.1. The test cell shall have a temperature set point equal to $\mathrm { T _ { r e g } }$ . The actual temperature value shall be within $\pm \nobreakspace 3 \nobreakspace ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ at the start of the test and within $\pm ~ 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ during the test.

3.2.1.2. The specific humidity (H) of either the air in the test cell or the intake air of the engine shall be such that:

$$
3 , 0 \le \mathrm { H } \le 8 , 1 \qquad \mathrm { ( g ~ H _ 2 O / k g ~ d r y ~ a i r ) }
$$

3.2.1.3. The air temperature and humidity shall be measured at the cooling fan outlet at a rate of $^ { 0 , 1 \mathrm { H z } }$ .

# 3.2.2. Soak area

3.2.2.1. The soak area shall have a temperature set point equal to $\mathrm { T _ { r e g } }$ and the actual temperature value shall be within $\pm \nobreakspace 3 \nobreakspace ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ on a 5 minute running arithmetic average and shall not show a systematic deviation from the set point. The temperature shall be measured continuously at a minimum frequency of $^ { 0 , 0 3 3 \mathrm { H z } }$ .

3.2.2.2. The location of the temperature sensor for the soak area shall be representative to measure the ambient temperature around the vehicle and shall be checked by the technical service.

The sensor shall be at least $1 0 \mathrm { { c m } }$ away from the wall of the soak area and shall be shielded from direct air flow.

The air-flow conditions within the soak room in the vicinity of the vehicle shall represent a natural convection flow representative for the dimension of the room (no forced convection).

3.3. Test vehicle

3.3.1. The vehicle to be tested shall be representative of the family for which the ATCT data are determined (as described in paragraph 2.1. of this Sub-Annex 6a).

3.3.2. From the ATCT Family, the Interpolation Family with the lowest engine capacity shall be selected (see paragraph 2 of this Sub-Annex 6a), and the test vehicle shall be in the ‘vehicle $\mathrm { H } '$ configuration of this family.

3.3.3. Where applicable, the vehicle with the lowest enthalpy of the active heat storage device and the slowest heat release for the active heat storage device from the ATCT Family shall be selected.

3.3.4. The test vehicle shall meet the requirements detailed in paragraph 2.3. of Sub-Annex 6 and paragraph 2.1 of this Sub-Annex 6a.

3.4. Settings

3.4.1. Road load and dynamometer settings shall be as specified in SubAnnex 4, including the requirement for the room temperature to be at $2 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .

To take account of the difference in air density at $1 4 ~ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ when compared to the air density at $2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , the chassis dynamometer shall be set as specified in paragraphs 7. and 8. of Sub-Annex 4 with the exception that $\mathrm { f } _ { 2 \_ \mathrm { T R e g } }$ from the following equation shall be used as the target coefficient $\mathrm { C _ { t } }$ .

$$
\mathrm { f } _ { 2 \_ \mathrm { T R e g } } = \mathrm { f } _ { 2 } \times ( \mathrm { T _ { r e f } } + 2 7 3 ) / ( \mathrm { T _ { r e g } } + 2 7 3 )
$$

where:

f2 is the second order road load coefficient, at reference conditions, $\mathrm { { N } } / ( \mathrm { { k m } } / \mathrm { { h } } ) ^ { 2 }$ ;   
$\mathrm { T _ { r e f } }$ is the road load reference temperature as specified in paragraph 3.2.10. of this Annex, C;   
Treg is the regional temperature, as defined in paragraph 3.1.1., C.

In the case that a valid chassis dynamometer setting of the $2 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ test is available, the second order chassis dynamometer coefficient of $\mathrm { C _ { d } }$ shall be adapted in accordance with the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { C _ { d \_ T r e g } = C _ { d } + ( f _ { 2 \_ T R e g } - f _ { 2 } ) }
$$

3.4.2. The ATCT test and its road load setting shall be performed on a 2WD dynamometer in the case that the corresponding Type 1 test was done on a 2WD dynamometer; and it shall be performed on a 4WD dynamometer in the case that the corresponding Type 1 test was done on a 4WD dynamometer.

3.5. Preconditioning

At the request of the manufacturer preconditioning may be undertaken at Treg.

The engine temperature shall be within $\pm \ : 2 \ : ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ of the set point of $2 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ or $\mathrm { T _ { r e g } . }$ , whichever temperature is chosen for the preconditioning.

3.5.1. Pure ICE vehicles shall be preconditioned as described in paragraph 2.6. of Sub-Annex 6.

3.5.2. NOVC-HEVs shall be preconditioned as described in paragraph 3.3.1.1. of Sub-Annex 8.

3.5.3. OVC-HEVs shall be preconditioned as described in paragraph 2.1.1. or 2.1.2. of Appendix 4 to Sub-Annex 8.

3.6. Soak procedure

3.6.1. After preconditioning and before testing, vehicles shall be kept in a soak area with the ambient conditions described in paragraph 3.2.2. of this Sub-Annex 6a.

3.6.2. From the end of the preconditioning until the soaking at $T _ { r e g } ,$ the vehicle shall not be exposed to a different temperature than $T _ { r e g }$ for longer than 10 minutes.

3.6.3. The vehicle shall then be kept in the soak area such that the time from the end of the preconditioning test to the beginning of the ATCT test is equal to $\mathrm { t _ { s o a k \_ A T C T } }$ with a tolerance of an additional 15 minutes. At the request of the manufacturer, and upon approval of the approval authority, tsoak_ATCT can be extended by up to 120 minutes. In this case, the extended time shall be used for the cool down specified in paragraph 3.9. of this Sub-Annex 6a.

3.6.4. The soak shall be performed without using a cooling fan and with all body parts positioned as intended under normal parking operation. The time between the end of the preconditioning and the start of the ATCT test shall be recorded.

3.6.5. The transfer from the soak area to the test cell shall be undertaken as quickly as possible. The vehicle shall not be exposed to a temperature different from $\mathrm { T _ { r e g } }$ for longer than 10 minutes.

3.7. ATCT Test

3.7.1. The test cycle shall be the applicable WLTC specified in Sub-Annex 1 for that class of vehicle.

3.7.2. The procedures for undertaking the emissions test as specified in SubAnnex 6 for pure ICE vehicles and in Sub-Annex 8 for NOVC-HEVs and for the charge-sustaining Type 1 test of OVC-HEVs shall be followed, with the exception that the ambient conditions for the test cell shall be those as described in paragraph 3.2.1. of this Sub-Annex 6a.

3.7.3. In particular, the tailpipe emissions defined by Table A7/1 Step no.1 for pure ICE vehicles and Table A8/5 Step no.2 for HEVs at an ATCT test shall not exceed the Euro 6 emission limits applicable to the vehicle tested defined in Table 2 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 715/2007.

3.8. Calculation and Documentation

3.8.1. The family correction factor, $F C F$ , shall be calculated as follows:

$$
F C F = M _ { C O 2 , T r e g } / M _ { C O 2 , 2 3 ^ { \circ } }
$$

where

MCO2,23° is the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emission of the average of all applicable Type 1 tests at $2 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ of vehicle $\mathrm { H }$ , after Step 3 of Table A7/1 of Sub-Annex 7 for pure ICE vehicles and after Step   
3 of Table A8/5 for OVC-HEVs and NOVC-HEVs, but without any further corrections, $\mathrm { { g } / k m }$ ; MCO2,Treg is the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emission over the complete WLTC cycle of the test at regional temperature after Step 3 of Table A7/1 of Sub-Annex 7 for pure ICE vehicles and after Step   
3 of Table A8/5 for OVC-HEVs and NOVC-HEVs but without any further corrections, $\mathrm { { g / k m } }$ . For OVC-HEVs and NOVC-HEVs, the $\operatorname { K } _ { \mathbf { C O 2 } }$ factor as defined in SubAnnex 8 Appendix 2 shall be used.

Both $\mathrm { M } _ { \mathrm { C O 2 } , 2 3 ^ { \circ } }$ and $\mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O } 2 , \mathrm { T r e g } }$ shall be measured on the same test vehicle.

The $F C F$ shall be included in all relevant test reports.

The $F C F$ shall be rounded to 4 points of decimal.

3.8.2. The $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ values for each pure ICE vehicle within the ATCT Family (as defined in paragraph 2.3. of this Sub-Annex 6a) shall be calculated using the following equations:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { M _ { C O 2 , c , 5 } = M _ { C O 2 , c , 4 } \times F C F } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { M _ { C O 2 , p , 5 } = M _ { C O 2 , p , 4 } \times F C F } } \end{array}
$$

where

$M _ { C O 2 , c , 4 }$ and $M _ { C O 2 , p , 4 }$ are the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions over the complete WLTC, c, and the cycle phases, p, resulting from the previous calculation step, $\mathrm { { g / k m } }$ ;

$M _ { C O 2 , c , 5 }$ and $M _ { C O 2 , p , 5 }$ are the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions over the complete WLTC, c, and the cycle phases, p, including the ATCT correction, and shall be used for any further corrections or any further calculations, $\mathrm { { g / k m } }$ ;

3.8.3. The $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ values for each OVC-HEV and NOVC-HEV within the ATCT Family (as defined in paragraph 2.3. of this Sub-Annex 6a) shall be calculated using the following equations:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { M _ { C O 2 , C S , c , 5 } = M _ { C O 2 , C S , c , 4 } \times F C F } \\ { \ } \\ { M _ { C O 2 , C S , p , 5 } = M _ { C O 2 , C S , p , 4 } \times F C F } \end{array}
$$

where

$M _ { C O 2 , C S , c , 4 }$ and $M _ { C O 2 , C S , p , 4 }$ are the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions over the complete WLTC, c, and the cycle phases, p, resulting from the previous calculation step, $\mathrm { { g / k m } }$ ;

$M _ { C O 2 , C S , c , 5 }$ and $M _ { C O 2 , C S , p , 5 }$ are the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions over the complete WLTC, c, and the cycle phases, p, including the ATCT correction, and shall be used for any further corrections or any further calculations, $\mathrm { { g } / k m }$ .

3.8.4. If a $F C F$ is less than one, it is deemed to be equal to one, in the case of the worstcase approach, in accordance with paragraph 4.1 of this SubAnnex.

3.9. Provision for cool down

3.9.1. For the test vehicle serving as a reference vehicle for the ATCT Family and all vehicles $\mathrm { H }$ of the interpolation families within the ATCT Family, the end temperature of the engine coolant shall be measured after soaking at $2 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for the duration of $\mathrm { t } _ { \mathrm { s o a k \_ A T C T } }$ , with a tolerance of an additional 15 minutes, having beforehand driven the respective Type 1 test at $2 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . The duration is measured from the end of that respective Type 1 test.

3.9.1.1. In the case that $\mathrm { t _ { s o a k \_ A T C T } }$ was extended in the respective ATCT test, the same soaking time shall be used, with a tolerance of an additional 15 minutes.

3.9.2. The cool down procedure shall be undertaken as soon as possible after the end of the Type 1 test, with a maximum delay of 20 minutes. The measured soaking time is the time between the measurement of the end temperature and the end of the Type 1 test at $2 3 \ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , and shall be included in all relevant test sheets.

3.9.3. The average temperature of the soak area of the last 3 hours shall be subtracted from the measured temperature of the engine coolant at the end of the soaking time specified in paragraph 3.9.1. This is referred to as $\Delta _ { \mathrm { T } \_ \mathrm { A T C T } }$ , rounded to the nearest whole number.

3.9.4. If $\Delta _ { \mathrm { T } \_ \mathrm { A T C T } }$ is higher or equal than $- 2 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ from the test vehicle $\Delta _ { \mathrm { T \_ A T C T } }$ this Interpolation Family shall be considered to be a member of the same ATCT Family.

3.9.5. For all vehicles within an ATCT Family the coolant shall be measured at the same location in the cooling system. That location shall be as close as possible to the engine so that the coolant temperature is as representative as possible to the engine temperature.

3.9.6. The measurement of the temperature of the soak areas shall be as specified in paragraph 3.2.2.2. of this Sub-Annex 6a.

4. Alternatives in the measurement process

4.1. Worst case approach vehicle cool down

On request by the manufacturer and with approval by the approval authority, the Type 1 Test procedure for cool down may be applied instead of provisions of paragraph 3.6 of this Sub-Annex 6a. For that purpose:

(a) The provisions of paragraph 2.7.2. of Sub-Annex 6 shall apply with the additional requirement of a minimum soak time of 9 hours.

(b) The engine temperature shall be within $\pm \ : 2 \ : ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ of the set point $\mathrm { T _ { r e g } }$ before the start of the ATCT test. That temperature shall be included in all relevant test sheets. In this case, the provision for cool down described in paragraph 3.9. of this Sub-Annex 6a and the criteria on engine compartment insulation can be skipped for all vehicles in the family.

This alternative is not allowed if the vehicle is equipped with an active heat storage device.

The application of that approach shall be included in all relevant test reports.

4.2. ATCT family composed of a single Interpolation family

In the case, that the ATCT family consists of only one interpolation family, the provision for cool down described in paragraph 3.9. of this Sub-Annex 6a can be skipped. This shall be included in all relevant test reports.

4.3. Alternative engine temperature measurement

In the case that measuring the coolant temperature is not feasible, on request of the manufacturer and with approval of the approval authority, instead of using the coolant temperature for the provision for cool down described in paragraph 3.9. of this Sub-Annex 6a, the engine oil temperature may be used. In that case, for all vehicles within the family the engine oil temperature shall be used.

The application of that procedure shall be included in all relevant test reports.

# Correction of $\mathbf { C O } _ { 2 }$ results against the target speed and distance

# 1. General

This Sub-Annex 6b defines the specific provisions regarding the correction of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ test results for tolerances against the target speed and distance.

This Sub-Annex 6b applies to pure ICE vehicles only.

# 2. Vehicle speed measurement

2.1. The actual/measured vehicle speed $\mathrm { ( v _ { m i } ; \ k m / h ) }$ ) coming from the roller speed of the chassis dynamometer shall be sampled with a measurement frequency of $1 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ together with the actual time that corresponds to the actual speed.

2.2. The target speed $\mathrm { \check { v } _ { i } ; k m / h \rangle }$ ) between time points in Tables A1/1 to A1/12 in Sub-Annex 1 shall be determined by a linear interpolation method at a frequency of $1 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ .

# 3. Correction procedure

3.1. Calculation of the actual/measured and target power at the wheels

The power and the forces at the wheels from the target and actual/ measured speed shall be calculated by applying the following equations:

$$
F _ { i } = f _ { 0 } + f _ { 1 } \times \frac { \left( V _ { i } + V _ { i - 1 } \right) } { 2 } + f _ { 2 } \times \frac { \left( V _ { i } + V _ { i - 1 } \right) ^ { 2 } } { 4 } + \left( \mathrm { T M } + m _ { r } \right) \times a _ { i }
$$

$$
P _ { i } = F _ { i } \times \frac { \left( V _ { i } + V _ { i - 1 } \right) } { 3 , 6 \times 2 } \times 0 , 0 0 1
$$

$$
F _ { m i } = f _ { 0 } + f _ { 1 } \times \frac { \left( V m _ { i } + V m _ { i - 1 } \right) } { 2 } + f _ { 2 } \times \frac { \left( V m _ { i } + V m _ { i - 1 } \right) ^ { 2 } } { 4 } + \left( \mathbf { T M } + m _ { r } \right) \times a _ { m i }
$$

$$
P _ { m i } = F _ { m i } \times \frac { \left( V m _ { i } + V m _ { i - 1 } \right) } { 3 , 6 \times 2 } \times 0 , 0 0 1
$$

$$
a _ { i } = \frac { ( V _ { i } - V _ { i - 1 } ) } { 3 , 6 \times ( t _ { i } - t _ { i - 1 } ) }
$$

$$
a _ { m i } = \frac { ( V m _ { i } - V m _ { i - 1 } ) } { 3 , 6 \times ( t _ { i } - t _ { i - 1 } ) }
$$

where:

$F _ { i }$ is the target driving force during the period from $( \mathrm { i } - 1 )$ to (i), N;   
$F _ { m i }$ is the actual/measured driving force during the period from $( \mathrm { i } -$ 1) to (i), N;   
$P _ { i }$ is the target power during the period from (i – 1) to (i), kW;   
$P _ { m i }$ is the actual/measured power during the period from $( \mathrm { i } - 1 )$ to (i), kW;   
$f _ { 0 } , f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 }$ are the road load coefficients from Sub-Annex 4, N, $\mathrm { { N / { ( k m / h ) } } }$ , $\mathrm { { N } } / ( \mathrm { { k m } } / \mathrm { { h } } ) ^ { 2 }$ ;   
$V _ { i }$ is the target speed at time (i); $\mathrm { { k m / h } }$ ;   
$V m _ { i }$ is the actual/measured speed at time (i); $\mathrm { { k m / h } }$ ;   
TM is the test mass of the vehicle, kg;   
$m _ { r }$ is the equivalent effective mass of rotating components in accordance with paragraph 2.5.1. of Sub-Annex 4, kg;   
$a _ { i }$ is the target acceleration during the period from (i-1) to (i), $\mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ ;   
ami is the actual/measured acceleration during the period from (i – 1) to (i), $\mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ ;   
$t _ { i }$ is the time, s.

3.2. In the next step an initial POVERRUN,1 is calculated using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { P _ { O V E R R U N , 1 } } = - \ 0 { , } 0 2 \times \ \mathrm { P _ { R A T E D } }
$$

where: POVERRUN,1 is the initial overrun power, kW; PRATED is the rated vehicle power, kW.

3.3. All calculated $P _ { i }$ and $P _ { m i }$ values that are below $\mathrm { P _ { O V E R R U N , 1 } }$ shall be set to POVERRUN,1 in order to exclude negative values not relevant for the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions.

3.4. The $P _ { m , j }$ values shall be calculated for each individual phase of the WLTC using the following equation:

$$
P _ { m , j } = \sum _ { t _ { 0 } } ^ { t _ { e n d } } P _ { m i } / \mathrm { n }
$$

where:

$P _ { m , j }$ is the average actual/measured power of the considered phase j, kW;   
Pmi is the actual/measured power during the period from $( \mathrm { i } - 1 )$ to (i), kW;   
$t _ { 0 }$ is the time at the beginning of the considered phase j, s;   
$t _ { e n d }$ is the time at the end of the considered phase j, s;   
n is the number of time steps in the considered phase;   
j is the index number for the considered phase.

3.5. The average RCB corrected $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions $( \mathrm { { g } / k m ) }$ for each phase of the applicable WLTC shall be expressed in units $\mathrm { g / s }$ using the following equation:

$$
M _ { C O 2 , j } = M _ { C O 2 , R C B , j } \times \frac { d _ { m , j } } { t _ { j } }
$$

where:

MCO2,j is the average $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emission of phase j, g/s;   
MCO2,RCB,j is the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emission from step 1 of Table A7/1 of Sub-Annex 7 for the considered WLTC phase j corrected in accordance with Appendix 2 to Sub-Annex 6, and with the requirement of applying the RCB correction without considering the correction criterion c;   
dm,j is the actually driven distance of the considered phase j, km; is the duration of considered phase j, s.

3.6. In the next step these $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions $\mathrm { ( g / s ) }$ for each phase of the WLTC shall be correlated to the average $P _ { m , j 1 }$ values calculated in accordance with paragraph 3.4. of this Sub-Annex 6b.

The best fit of the data shall be calculated using the least square regression method. An example for this regression line (Veline line) is shown in Figure A6b $/ 1$ .

3.7. The vehicle specific Veline equation-1 calculated from paragraph 3.6. of this Sub-Annex 6b defines the correlation between $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions in $\mathrm { g / s }$ for the considered phase $\mathrm { j }$ and the average measured power at the wheel for the same phase $\mathrm { j }$ and is expressed with the following equation:

$$
M _ { C O 2 , j } = ( \mathrm { k } _ { \mathrm { v } , 1 } \times P _ { m , j 1 } ) + \mathrm { D } _ { \mathrm { v } , 1 }
$$

where:

$M _ { C O 2 , j }$ is the average $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emission of phase j, g/s;   
Pm,j1 is the average actual/measured power of the considered phase j calculated using POVERRUN,1, kW;   
$\mathbf { k } _ { \mathrm { v } , 1 }$ is the slope of the Veline equation-1, g $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { k W } \mathrm { s }$ ;   
$\mathrm { D } _ { \mathrm { v } , 1 }$ is the constant of the Veline equation-1, g $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { s }$ .

3.8. In the next step, a second POVERRUN,2 is calculated following the equation: $\mathrm { P _ { O V E R R U N , 2 } = - \Delta D _ { v , 1 } / \Delta k _ { v , 1 } }$ where: POVERRUN,2 is the second overrun power, kW; $\mathbf { k } _ { \mathrm { v } , 1 }$ is the slope of the Veline equation-1, g $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { k W s }$ ; $\mathrm { D } _ { \mathrm { v } , 1 }$ is the constant of the Veline equation-1, g $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { s }$ .

3.9. All calculated $P _ { i }$ and $P _ { m i }$ values from paragraph 3.1. of this Sub-Annex 6b that are below POVERRUN,2 shall be set to POVERRUN,2 in order to exclude negative values not relevant for the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions.

3.10. The $P _ { m , j 2 }$ values shall be computed again for each individual phase of the WLTC using the equations from paragraph 3.4. of this Sub-Annex 6b.

3.11. New vehicle specific Veline equation-2 shall be computed using the least square regression method described in paragraph 3.6. of this Sub-Annex 6b. The Veline equation-2 is expressed with the following equation:

$$
M _ { C O 2 , j } = ( \mathrm { k } _ { \mathrm { v } , 2 } \times P _ { m , j 2 } ) + \mathrm { D } _ { \mathrm { v } , 2 }
$$

where:

$\begin{array} { r } { M _ { C O } } \\ { P _ { m , j 2 } } \\ { \phantom { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \\ { \mathrm { k _ { v , 2 } } } \\ { \phantom { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \\ { \mathrm { D _ { v , 2 } } } \end{array}$ is the average $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emission of phase j, g/s;   
is the average actual/measured power of the considered phase j calculated using POVERRUN,2, kW;   
is the slope of the Veline equation-2, g $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { k W } \mathrm { s }$ ;   
is the constant of the Veline equation-2, g $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { s }$ .

3.12. In the next step, the $P _ { i , j }$ values coming from the target speed profile shall be calculated for each individual phase of the WLTC using the following equation:

$$
P _ { i , j 2 } = \sum _ { t _ { 0 } } ^ { t _ { e n d } } P _ { i , 2 } / \mathrm { n }
$$

where:

$P _ { i , j 2 }$ is the average target power of the considered phase j calculated using POVERRUN,2, kW;   
$P _ { i , 2 }$ is the target power during the period from $( \mathrm { i } - 1 )$ to (i) calculated using POVERRUN,2, kW;   
$t _ { 0 }$ is the time at the beginning of the considered phase j, s;   
$t _ { e n d }$ is the time at the end of the considered phase j, s;   
n is the number of time steps in the considered phase;   
j is the index number for the considered WLTC phase.

3.13. Delta in $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions of period $\mathrm { j }$ expressed in $\mathrm { g / s }$ is then calculated following the equation:

$$
\Delta \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 , \mathrm { j } } = \mathrm { k } _ { \mathrm { v } , 2 } \times ( P _ { i , j 2 } - P _ { m , j 2 } )
$$

where:

$\Delta \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 , \mathrm { j } }$ is the delta in $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions of period j expressed, $\mathrm { g / s }$ ;   
kv,2 is the slope of the Veline equation-2, g $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { k W } \mathrm { s }$ ;   
$P _ { i , j 2 }$ is the average target power of the considered period $\mathrm { j }$ calculated using POVERRUN,2, kW;   
Pm,j2 is the average actual/measured power of the considered period j calculated using POVERRUN,2, kW;   
j is the considered period $\mathrm { j }$ and it can be the cycle phase or the total cycle.

3.14. The final distance and speed corrected $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions of period $\mathrm { j }$ is calculated following the equation:

$$
M _ { C O 2 , j , 2 b } = \left( \Delta \mathrm { C O _ { 2 , j } } + M _ { C O 2 , j , 1 } \times \frac { d _ { m , j } } { t _ { j } } \right) \times t _ { j } / d _ { i , j }
$$

where:

$M _ { C O 2 , j , 2 , b }$ is distance and speed corrected $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions of period j, $\mathrm { { g / k m } }$ ;   
MCO2,j,1 is $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions of period j of step 1, see Table A7/1 in Sub-Annex $7 , \ \mathrm { g / k m }$ ; $\Delta \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 , \mathrm { j } }$ is the delta in $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ mass emissions of period j expressed, g/s;   
$t _ { j }$ is the duration of considered period j, s;   
$d _ { m , j }$ is the actually driven distance of the considered phase j, km;   
$d _ { i , j }$ is the target distance of the considered period j, km;   
j is the considered period ${ \mathrm { j } } ,$ which can either be the cycle phase or the total cycle.

# Calculations

1. General requirements   
1.1. Calculations related specifically to hybrid, pure electric and compressed hydrogen fuel cell vehicles are described in SubAnnex 8. A stepwise procedure for calculating test results is described in paragraph 4. of Sub-Annex 8.   
1.2. The calculations described in this Sub-Annex shall be used for vehicles using combustion engines.   
1.3. Rounding of test results   
1.3.1. Intermediate steps in the calculations shall not be rounded.   
1.3.2. The final criteria emission results shall be rounded in one step to the number of places to the right of the decimal point indicated by the applicable emission standard plus one additional significant figure.   
1.3.3. The $\mathrm { N O } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ correction factor, KH, shall be rounded to two decimal places.   
1.3.4. The dilution factor, DF, shall be rounded to two decimal places.   
1.3.5. For information not related to standards, good engineering judgement shall be used.   
1.3.6. Rounding of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and fuel consumption results is described in paragraph 1.4. of this Sub-Annex.   
1.4. ►M3 Stepwise procedure for calculating the final test results for vehicles using combustion engines ◄ The results shall be calculated in the order described in Table A7/1. All applicable results in the column ‘Output’ shall be recorded. The column ‘Process’ describes the paragraphs to be used for calculation or contains additional calculations. For the purpose of this table, the following nomenclature within the equations and results is used: c complete applicable cycle; p every applicable cycle phase; i every applicable criteria emission component, without $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ ;   
$\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emission.

Determination of diluted exhaust gas volume

Volume calculation for a variable dilution device capable of operating at a constant or variable flow rate

The volumetric flow shall be measured continuously. The total volume shall be measured for the duration of the test.

Volume calculation for a variable dilution device using a positive displacement pump

The volume shall be calculated using the following equation:

$$
{ \mathrm { V } } = { \mathrm { V } } _ { 0 } \times { \mathrm { N } }
$$

where:

V is the volume of the diluted gas, in litres per test (prior to correction);

$\mathrm { V } _ { 0 }$ is the volume of gas delivered by the positive displacement pump in testing conditions, litres per pump revolution;

N is the number of revolutions per test.

2.2.1.1. Correcting the volume to standard conditions

The diluted exhaust gas volume, V, shall be corrected to standard conditions according to the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { { V } _ { \mathrm { { m i x } } } = V \times \mathrm { { K } _ { 1 } \times \left( \frac { \mathrm { { P } _ { B } - P _ { 1 } } } { T _ { p } } \right) } }
$$

where:

$$
\mathrm { K } _ { 1 } = \frac { 2 7 3 , 1 5 ( \mathrm { K } ) } { 1 0 1 , 3 2 5 ( \mathrm { k P a } ) } = 2 , 6 9 6 1
$$

$\mathrm { P _ { B } }$ is the test room barometric pressure, $\mathrm { k P a }$ ;   
$\mathrm { { P } } _ { 1 }$ is the vacuum at the inlet of the positive displacement pump relative to the ambient barometric pressure, kPa;   
$\mathrm { { T _ { p } } }$ is the arithmetic average temperature of the diluted exhaust gas entering the positive displacement pump during the test, Kelvin (K).

3.

Mass emissions

General requirements

Assuming no compressibility effects, all gases involved in the engine's intake, combustion and exhaust processes may be considered to be ideal according to Avogadro’s hypothesis.

The mass, M of gaseous compounds emitted by the vehicle during the test shall be determined by the product of the volumetric concentration of the gas in question and the volume of the diluted exhaust gas with due regard for the following densities under the reference conditions of $\bar { 2 7 3 } , 1 5 \ : \mathrm { K } \ : ( 0 \ : ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and $1 0 \bar { 1 } , 3 2 5 \mathrm { k P a }$ :

Carbon monoxide (CO) $\rho = 1 , 2 5 \mathrm { g } / 1$ Carbon dioxide $\left( \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } \right)$ $\rho = 1 , 9 6 4 \mathrm { g } / 1$

Hydrocarbons:

for petrol (E10) $( \mathrm { C } _ { 1 } \mathrm { H } _ { 1 , 9 3 } \mathrm { ~ O } _ { 0 , 0 3 3 } )$ ρ ¼ 0,646g=l

for LPG $\mathrm { ( C _ { 1 } H } _ { 2 , 5 2 5 } \mathrm { ) }$

for NG/biomethane $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 4 } )$ ρ ¼ 0,716g=l

Nitrogen oxides $\mathrm { ( N O _ { x } ) }$

The density for NMHC mass calculations shall be equal to that of total hydrocarbons at $2 7 3 , 1 5 \mathrm { ~ K ~ }$ $( 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and $^ { 1 0 1 , 3 2 5 \mathrm { ~ k P a ~ } }$ , and is fuel-dependent. The density for propane mass calculations (see paragraph 3.5. in Sub-Annex 5) is $1 { , } 9 6 7 \ \mathrm { g } / 1$ at standard conditions.

If a fuel type is not listed in this paragraph, the density of that fuel shall be calculated using the equation given in paragraph 3.1.3. of this Sub-Annex.

3.1.3.

The general equation for the calculation of total hydrocarbon density for each reference fuel with an mean composition of $\mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { X } } \mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { Y } } \mathrm { O } _ { Z }$ is as follows:

$$
\rho _ { \mathrm { T H C } } = \frac { \mathrm { M W _ { C } } + \displaystyle \frac { \mathrm { H } } { C } \times \mathrm { M W _ { H } } + \frac { \mathrm { O } } { C } \times \mathrm { M W _ { O } } } { \mathrm { V _ { M } } }
$$

where:

ρTHC is the density of total hydrocarbons and non-methane hydrocarbons, $\mathrm { g } / \mathrm { l }$ ;   
$\mathrm { M W _ { C } }$ is the molar mass of carbon $( 1 2 , 0 1 1 \ \mathrm { g / m o l } )$ ;   
$\mathbf { M W } _ { \mathrm { H } }$ is the molar mass of hydrogen (1,008 g/mol);   
MWO is the molar mass of oxygen $\mathrm { 1 5 , 9 9 9 { \mathrm { ~ g / m o l } } ) }$ ;   
$\mathrm { V _ { M } }$ is the molar volume of an ideal gas at 273,15 K $\mathrm { 0 ^ { \circ } C ) }$ and 101,325 kPa (22,413 l/mol);   
H/C is the hydrogen to carbon ratio for a specific fuel $\mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { X } } \mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { Y } } \mathrm { O } _ { Z }$ ;   
O/C is the oxygen to carbon ratio for a specific fuel $\mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { X } } \mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { Y } } \mathrm { O } _ { Z }$ .

# 3.2.

Mass emissions calculation

3.2.1.

Mass emissions of gaseous compounds per cycle phase shall be calculated using the following equations:

$$
\mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { i , p h a s e } } = \frac { \mathbf { V } _ { \mathrm { m i x , p h a s e } } \times \mathsf { p } _ { \mathrm { i } } \times \mathbf { K } \mathbf { H } _ { \mathrm { p h a s e } } \times \mathbf { C } _ { \mathrm { i , p h a s e } } \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 } } { \mathsf { d } _ { \mathrm { p h a s e } } }
$$

where:

$\mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { i } }$ is the mass emission of compound i per test or phase, $\mathrm { { g } / \mathrm { { k m } } }$ ;   
Vmix is the volume of the diluted exhaust gas per test or phase expressed in litres per test/phase and corrected to standard conditions $( 2 7 3 , 1 5 \mathrm { ~ K ~ } ( 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and $1 0 1 , 3 2 5 \ \mathrm { k P a } )$ ;   
$\rho _ { \mathrm { i } }$ is the density of compound i in grams per litre at standard temperature and pressure (273,15 K $( 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and 101,325 $\mathrm { k P a } )$ ;   
KH is a humidity correction factor applicable only to the mass emissions of oxides of nitrogen, $\mathrm { N O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ , per test or phase;   
Ci is the concentration of compound i per test or phase in the diluted exhaust gas expressed in ppm and corrected by the amount of compound i contained in the dilution air;   
d is the distance driven over the applicable WLTC, km;   
n is the number of phases of the applicable WLTC.

The concentration of a gaseous compound in the diluted exhaust gas shall be corrected by the amount of the gaseous compound in the dilution air using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { C _ { i } = C _ { e } - C _ { d } \times \left( 1 - \frac { 1 } { D F } \right) }
$$

where:

$\mathrm { C _ { i } }$ is the concentration of gaseous compound i in the diluted exhaust gas corrected by the amount of gaseous compound i contained in the dilution air, ppm;   
$\mathrm { C _ { e } }$ is the measured concentration of gaseous compound i in the diluted exhaust gas, ppm;   
$\mathrm { C _ { d } }$ is the concentration of gaseous compound i in the dilution air, ppm;   
DF is the dilution factor.

3.2.1.1.1. The dilution factor DF shall be calculated using the equation for the concerned fuel:

$\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathrm { D F } = \frac { \Phi } { \mathrm { C _ { e x t } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } } } \\ & { \mathrm { D F } = \frac { 1 3 \cdot \Phi } { \mathrm { C _ { e x t } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } } } \\ & { \mathrm { D F } = \frac { 1 1 } { \mathrm { C _ { e x t } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } } } \\ & { \mathrm { D F } = \frac { 9 \cdot \Phi } { \mathrm { C _ { e x t } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } } } \\ & { \mathrm { D F } = \frac { 9 \cdot \Phi } { \mathrm { C _ { e x t } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } } } \\ & { \mathrm { D F } = \frac { 1 2 \cdot \Phi } { \mathrm { C _ { e x t } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } } } \\ & { \mathrm { D F } = \frac { 1 } { \mathrm { C _ { e x t } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } + \mathrm { C _ { m a x } } } } \end{array}$ for petrol (E10) for diesel (B7) for LPG for NG/biomethane for ethanol (E85) for hydrogen

With respect to the equation for hydrogen:

CH2O is the concentration of $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { _ 2 O }$ in the diluted exhaust gas contained in the sample bag, per cent volume;   
CH2O-DA is the concentration of $_ \mathrm { H } \mathrm { _ 2 O }$ in the dilution air, per cent volume;   
CH2 is the concentration of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ in the diluted exhaust gas contained in the sample bag, ppm.

If a fuel type is not listed in this paragraph, the DF for that fuel shall be calculated using the equations in paragraph 3.2.1.1.2. of this Sub-Annex.

If the manufacturer uses a DF that covers several phases, it shall calculate a DF using the mean concentration of gaseous compounds for the phases concerned.

The mean concentration of a gaseous compound shall be calculated using the following equation:

$$
\overline { { \mathrm { C } } } _ { \mathrm { i } } = \frac { \sum _ { \mathrm { p h a s e } = 1 } ^ { \mathrm { n } } ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { i , p h a s e } } \times \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { m i x , p h a s e } } ) } { \sum _ { \mathrm { p h a s e } = 1 } ^ { \mathrm { n } } \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { m i x , p h a s e } } }
$$

where:

$\mathrm { C _ { i } }$ is mean concentration of a gaseous compound;   
$\mathrm { C _ { i , p h a s e } }$ is the concentration of each phase;   
$\mathrm { V _ { m i x , p h a s e } }$ is the $\mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { m i x } }$ of the corresponding phase;

The general equation for calculating the dilution factor DF for each reference fuel with an arithmetic average composition of ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { \mathrm { x } } { \mathrm { H } } _ { \mathrm { y } } { \mathrm { O } } _ { \mathrm { z } }$ is as follows:

$$
\mathrm { D F } = \frac { \mathrm { X } } { \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { C O 2 } } + ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { H C } } + \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { C O } } ) \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } }
$$

where:

$$
\mathrm { X } = 1 0 0 \times \frac { \mathrm { x } } { \mathrm { x } + \frac { \mathrm { y } } { 2 } + 3 , 7 6 ( \mathrm { x } + \frac { \mathrm { y } } { 4 } - \frac { \mathrm { z } } { 2 } ) }
$$

$\mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { C O 2 } }$ is the concentration of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ in the diluted exhaust gas contained in the sample bag, per cent volume;

$\mathrm { C _ { H C } }$ is the concentration of HC in the diluted exhaust gas contained in the sample bag, ppm carbon equivalent;

CCO is the concentration of CO in the diluted exhaust gas contained in the sample bag, ppm.

# 3.2.1.1.3. Methane measurement

For methane measurement using a GC-FID, NMHC shall be calculated using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { C _ { N M H C } } = \mathrm { C _ { T H C } } - \left( \mathrm { R f _ { C H 4 } } \times \mathrm { C _ { C H 4 } } \right)
$$

where:

CNMHC is the corrected concentration of NMHC in the diluted exhaust gas, ppm carbon equivalent;   
CTHC is the concentration of THC in the diluted exhaust gas, ppm carbon equivalent and corrected by the amount of THC contained in the dilution air;   
$\mathrm { C _ { C H 4 } }$ is the concentration of $\mathrm { C _ { C H 4 } }$ in the diluted exhaust gas, ppm carbon equivalent and corrected by the amount of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ contained in the dilution air;

RfCH4 is the FID response factor to methane determined and specified in paragraph 5.4.3.2. of Sub-Annex 5.

3.2.1.1.3.2. For methane measurement using an NMC-FID, the calculation of NMHC depends on the calibration gas/method used for the zero/ calibration adjustment.

The FID used for the THC measurement (without NMC) shall be calibrated with propane/air in the normal manner.

For the calibration of the FID in series with an NMC, the following methods are permitted:

(a) The calibration gas consisting of propane/air bypasses the NMC;   
(b) The calibration gas consisting of methane/air passes through the NMC.

It is highly recommended to calibrate the methane FID with methane/air through the NMC.

In case (a), the concentration of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and NMHC shall be calculated using the following equations:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { C } _ { \mathrm { C H 4 } } = \frac { \mathbf { C } _ { \mathrm { H C ( w / N M C ) } } - \mathbf { C } _ { \mathrm { H C ( w / o N M C ) } } \times ( 1 - \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { E } } ) } { \mathbf { R } _ { \mathrm { f C H 4 } } \times ( \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { E } } - \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { M } } ) } } \\ { \mathbf { C } _ { \mathrm { N M H C } } = \frac { \mathbf { C } _ { \mathrm { H C ( w / o N M C ) } } \times ( 1 - \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { M } } ) - \mathbf { C } _ { \mathrm { H C ( w / N M C ) } } } { \mathbf { E } _ { \mathrm { E } } - \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { M } } } } \end{array}
$$

If $\mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { f C H 4 } } < 1 , 0 5$ , it may be omitted from the equation above for CCH4.

In case (b), the concentration of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and NMHC shall be calculated using the following equations:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathrm { \Delta C _ { C H 4 } } = \frac { \mathrm { \Delta C _ { H C ( w / N M C ) } } \times \mathrm { \Delta R _ { f C H 4 } } \times \mathrm { ( 1 - E _ { M } ) } - \mathrm { \Delta C _ { H C ( w / o N M C ) } } \times \mathrm { ( 1 - E _ { E } ) } } { \mathrm { \Delta R _ { f C H 4 } } \times \mathrm { ( E _ { E } - E _ { M } ) } } } \\ & { \mathrm { \Delta } } \\ & { \mathrm { \Delta C _ { N M H C } } = \frac { \mathrm { \Delta C _ { H C ( w / o N M C ) } } \times \mathrm { ( 1 - E _ { M } ) } - \mathrm { \Delta C _ { H C ( w / N M C ) } } \times \mathrm { R _ { f C H 4 } } \times \mathrm { ( 1 - E _ { M } ) } } { \mathrm { \Delta E _ { E } - E _ { M } } } } \end{array}
$$

where:

CHC(w/NMC) is the HC concentration with sample gas flowing through the NMC, ppm C;   
CHC(w/oNMC) is the HC concentration with sample gas bypassing the NMC, ppm C;   
RfCH4 is the methane response factor as determined per paragraph 5.4.3.2. of Sub-Annex 5;   
EM is the methane efficiency as determined per paragraph 3.2.1.1.3.3.1. of this Sub-Annex;

$\mathrm { E _ { E } }$ is the ethane efficiency as determined per paragraph 3.2.1.1.3.3.2. of this Sub-Annex.

If $\ R _ { \mathrm { f C H 4 } } < 1 , 0 5 $ , it may be omitted in the equations for case (b) above for $\mathrm { C _ { C H 4 } }$ and ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { \mathrm { N M H C } }$ .

3.2.1.1.3.3. Conversion efficiencies of the non-methane cutter, NMC

The NMC is used for the removal of the non-methane hydrocarbons from the sample gas by oxidizing all hydrocarbons except methane. Ideally, the conversion for methane is 0 per cent, and for the other hydrocarbons represented by ethane is 100 per cent. For the accurate measurement of NMHC, the two efficiencies shall be determined and used for the calculation of the NMHC emission.

# 3.2.1.1.3.3.1. Methane conversion efficiency, $\mathrm { E _ { M } }$

The methane/air calibration gas shall be flowed to the FID through the NMC and bypassing the NMC and the two concentrations recorded. The efficiency shall be determined using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { M } } = 1 - { \frac { \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { H C ( w / N M C ) } } } { \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { H C ( w / o N M C ) } } } }
$$

where:

CHC(w/NMC) is the HC concentration with $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ flowing through the NMC, ppm C;

CHC(w/oNMC) is the HC concentration with $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ bypassing the NMC, ppm C.

# 3.2.1.1.3.3.2. Ethane conversion efficiency, $\mathrm { E _ { E } }$

The ethane/air calibration gas shall be flowed to the FID through the NMC and bypassing the NMC and the two concentrations recorded. The efficiency shall be determined using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { E } } = 1 - { \frac { \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { H C ( w / N M C ) } } } { \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { H C ( w / o N M C ) } } } }
$$

where:

CHC(w/NMC) is the HC concentration with $\mathrm { C _ { 2 } H _ { 6 } }$ flowing through the NMC, ppm C;

CHC(w/oNMC) is the HC concentration with $\mathrm { C _ { 2 } H _ { 6 } }$ bypassing the NMC, ppm C.

If the ethane conversion efficiency of the NMC is 0,98 or above, $\mathrm { E _ { E } }$ shall be set to 1 for any subsequent calculation.

3.2.1.1.3.4. If the methane FID is calibrated through the cutter, $\mathrm { E _ { M } }$ shall be 0.

The equation to calculate $\mathrm { C _ { C H 4 } }$ in paragraph 3.2.1.1.3.2. (case (b)) in this Sub-Annex becomes:

$$
\mathrm { C _ { C H 4 } } = \mathrm { C _ { H C ( w / N M C ) } }
$$

The equation to calculate ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { \mathrm { N M H C } }$ in paragraph 3.2.1.1.3.2. (case (b)) in this Sub-Annex becomes:

$$
\mathrm { C _ { N M H C } = C _ { H C ( w / o N M C ) } - C _ { H C ( w / N M C ) } \times r _ { h } }
$$

The density used for NMHC mass calculations shall be equal to that of total hydrocarbons at 273,15 K $( 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and $1 0 1 { , } 3 2 5 \ \mathrm { k P a }$ and is fuel-dependent.

# 3.2.1.1.4. Flow-weighted arithmetic average concentration calculation

The following calculation method shall only be applied for CVS systems that are not equipped with a heat exchanger or for CVS systems with a heat exchanger that do not comply with paragraph 3.3.5.1. of Sub-Annex 5.

When the CVS flow rate, qvcvs, over the test varies by more than $\pm \nobreakspace 3 \nobreakspace$ per cent of the arithmetic average flow rate, a flow-weighted arithmetic average shall be used for all continuous diluted measurements including PN:

$$
\mathrm { C _ { \mathrm { e } } = \frac { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } q v c v s ( i ) \times \Delta t \times C ( i ) } { V } }
$$

where:

$\mathrm { C _ { e } }$ is the flow-weighted arithmetic average concentration;   
qvcvs(i) is the CVS flow rate at time $\mathrm { t } = \mathrm { i } \times \Delta \mathrm { t } , \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 } / \mathrm { m i n } .$ ;   
C(i) is the concentration at time ${ \mathrm { t } } = { \mathrm { i } } \times \Delta { \mathrm { t } } ,$ ppm;   
Δt sampling interval, s;   
V total CVS volume, $\mathfrak { m } ^ { 3 }$ .

3.2.1.2.

Calculation of the $\mathrm { N O } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ humidity correction factor

In order to correct the influence of humidity on the results of oxides of nitrogen, the following calculations apply:

$$
\mathrm { K H } = { \frac { 1 } { 1 - 0 , 0 3 2 9 \times ( \mathrm { H } - 1 0 , 7 1 ) } }
$$

where:

$$
\mathrm { H } = \frac { 6 , 2 1 1 \times \mathrm { R _ { a } } \times \mathrm { P _ { d } } } { \mathrm { P _ { B } } - \mathrm { P _ { d } } \times \mathrm { R _ { a } } \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } }
$$

and:

H is the specific humidity, grams of water vapour per kilogram dry air;

$\mathrm { R _ { a } }$ is the relative humidity of the ambient air, per cent; $\mathrm { P _ { d } }$ is the saturation vapour pressure at ambient temperature, kPa; $\mathrm { P _ { B } }$ is the atmospheric pressure in the room, kPa. The KH factor shall be calculated for each phase of the test cycle. The ambient temperature and relative humidity shall be defined as the arithmetic average of the continuously measured values during each phase.   
3.2.2. Determination of the HC mass emissions from compressionignition engines   
3.2.2.1. To calculate HC mass emission for compression-ignition engines, the arithmetic average HC concentration shall be calculated using the following equation: $\mathrm { C _ { \mathrm { e } } = \frac { \int _ { t _ { l } } ^ { t _ { 2 } } \mathrm { C _ { H C } \ d t } } { \Delta t _ { 2 } - t _ { l } } }$ where: $\begin{array} { r l } {  { \int _ { \mathrm { t } _ { 1 } } ^ { \mathrm { t } _ { 2 } } \mathbf { C } _ { \mathrm { H C } } \mathrm { d t } } } \end{array}$ is the integral of the recording of the heated FID over the test $\mathrm { t } _ { 1 }$ to $\mathrm { t } _ { 2 }$ ); $\mathrm { C _ { e } }$ is the concentration of HC measured in the diluted exhaust in ppm of $\mathrm { C _ { i } }$ and is substituted for $\mathrm { C _ { H C } }$ in all relevant equations.

3.2.3.2.2.2.1. The actual RRC values for the selected tyres on test vehicle L, $\mathrm { R R } _ { \mathrm { L } } ,$ and test vehicle H, ${ \mathrm { R R } } _ { \mathrm { H } } .$ shall be used as input for the interpolation method. See paragraph 4.2.2.1. of Sub-Annex 4.

If the tyres on the front and rear axles of vehicle L or H have different RRC values, the weighted mean of the rolling resistances shall be calculated using the equation in paragraph 3.2.3.2.2.2.3. of this Sub-Annex.

3.2.3.2.2.2.2. For the tyres fitted to an individual vehicle, the value of the rolling resistance coefficient $\mathrm { R R } _ { \mathrm { i n d } }$ shall be set to the RRC value of the applicable tyre energy efficiency class in accordance with Table A4/2 of Sub-Annex 4.

In the case where individual vehicles may be supplied with a complete set of standard wheels and tyres and a complete set of snow tyres (marked with 3 Peaked Mountain and Snowflake – 3PMS) with or without wheels, the additional wheels/tyres shall not be considered as optional equipment.

If the tyres on the front and rear axles belong to different energy efficiency classes, the weighted mean shall be used and calculated using the equation in paragraph 3.2.3.2.2.2.3. of this Sub-Annex.

If the same tyres, or tyres with the same rolling resistance coefficient were fitted to test vehicles $\mathrm { L }$ and H, the value of $\mathrm { R R } _ { \mathrm { i n d } }$ for the interpolation method shall be set to $\mathrm { R R } _ { \mathrm { H } }$ .

3.2.3.2.2.3. Aerodynamic drag of an individual vehicle

3.2.3.2.2.3.1. Determination of aerodynamic influence of optional equipment

The aerodynamic drag shall be measured for each of the aerodynamic drag-influencing items of optional equipment and body shapes in a wind tunnel fulfilling the requirements of paragraph 3.2. of Sub-Annex 4 verified by the approval authority.

3.2.3.2.2.3.2. Alternative method for determination of aerodynamic influence of optional equipment

At the request of the manufacturer and with approval of the approval authority, an alternative method (e.g. simulation, wind tunnel not fulfilling the criteria in Sub-Annex 4) may be used to determine $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \times \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } )$ if the following criteria are fulfilled:

(a) The alternative method shall fulfil an accuracy for $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \times \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } )$ of $\pm \ : 0 , 0 1 5 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ and, additionally, in the case that simulation is used, the Computational Fluid Dynamics method should be validated in detail such that the actual air flow patterns around the body, including magnitudes of flow velocities, forces, or pressures, are shown to match the validation test results;

(b) The alternative method shall be used only for those aerodynamic-influencing parts (e.g. wheels, body shapes, cooling system) for which equivalency was demonstrated;   
(c) Evidence of equivalency shall be shown in advance to the approval authority for each road load family in the case that a mathematical method is used, or every four years in the case that a measurement method is used, and in any case shall be based on wind tunnel measurements fulfilling the criteria of this Annex;   
(d) If the $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \times \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } )$ of a particular item of optional equipment is more than double the value of the optional equipment for which the evidence was given, aerodynamic drag shall not be determined by the alternative method; and   
(e) In the case that a simulation model is changed, a revalidation shall be necessary.   
3.2.3.2.2.3.3. Application of aerodynamic influence on the individual vehicle $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \times \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } ) _ { \mathrm { i n d } }$ is the difference in the product of the aerodynamic drag coefficient multiplied by frontal area between an individual vehicle and test vehicle L due to options and body shapes on the vehicle that differ from those of test vehicle $\mathrm { L } , \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ ; These differences in aerodynamic drag, $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \ \times \ \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } )$ , shall be determined with an accuracy of $\pm \ 0 , 0 1 5 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ . $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \ \times \ \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } ) _ { \mathrm { i n d } }$ may be calculated using the following equation maintaining the accuracy of $\pm \ : \ : 0 , 0 1 5 \ : \mathrm { \dot { m } } ^ { 2 }$ also for the sum of items of optional equipment and body shapes: $\Delta ( \mathrm { C _ { D } \times A _ { f } ) _ { i n d } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \Delta ( C _ { D } \times A _ { f } ) _ { i } }$ where: CD is the aerodynamic drag coefficient; $\mathbf { A } _ { \mathrm { f } }$ is the frontal area of the vehicle, $\mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ ; n is the number of items of optional equipment on the vehicle that are different between an individual vehicle and test vehicle L; $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \times \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } ) _ { \mathrm { i } }$ is the difference in the product of the aerodynamic drag coefficient multiplied by frontal area due to an individual feature, i, on the vehicle and is positive for an item of optional equipment that adds aerodynamic drag with respect to test vehicle $\mathrm { L }$ and vice versa, $\mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ . The sum of all $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \ \times \ \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } ) _ { \mathrm { i } }$ differences between test vehicles $\mathrm { L }$ and $\mathrm { H }$ shall correspond to $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \ \times$ Af)LH.   
3.2.3.2.2.3.4. Definition of complete aerodynamic delta between test vehicles H

and L

The total difference of the aerodynamic drag coefficient multiplied by frontal area between test vehicles L and H shall be referred to as $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \ \times \ \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } ) _ { \mathrm { L H } }$ and shall be included in all the relevant test reports, $\mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ .

# 3.2.3.2.2.3.5. Documentation of aerodynamic influences

The increase or decrease of the product of the aerodynamic drag coefficient multiplied by frontal area expressed as $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \times \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } )$ for all items of optional equipment and body shapes in the interpolation family that:

(a) have an influence on the aerodynamic drag of the vehicle; and (b) are to be included in the interpolation, shall be included in all relevant test reports, $\mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ .

3.2.3.2.2.3.6. Additional provisions for aerodynamic influences

The aerodynamic drag of vehicle $\mathrm { H }$ shall be applied to the whole interpolation family and $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \ \times \ \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } ) _ { \mathrm { L H } }$ shall be set to zero, if:

(a) the wind tunnel facility is not able to accurately determine $\Delta ( \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { D } } \times \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { f } } )$ ; or   
(b) there are no drag-influencing items of optional equipment between the test vehicles $\mathrm { H }$ and $\mathrm { L }$ that are to be included in the interpolation method.

3.2.3.2.2.4. Calculation of road load coefficients for individual vehicles

The road load coefficients $\mathrm { f _ { 0 } , ~ f _ { 1 } }$ and $\mathrm { f } _ { 2 }$ (as defined in SubAnnex 4) for test vehicles $\mathrm { H }$ and $\mathrm { L }$ are referred to as $\mathrm { f _ { 0 , H } , \ f _ { 1 , H } }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { f } _ { 2 , \mathrm { H } } , } \end{array}$ and $\mathrm { f _ { 0 , L } } ,$ $\mathrm { f _ { 1 , L } }$ and $\mathrm { f } _ { 2 , \mathrm { L } }$ respectively. An adjusted road load curve for the test vehicle $\mathrm { L }$ is defined as follows:

$$
\mathrm { F _ { L } } ( \mathbf { v } ) = \mathrm { f _ { 0 , L } ^ { * } } + \mathrm { f _ { 1 , H } } \times \mathbf { v } + \mathbf { f _ { 2 , L } ^ { * } } \times \mathbf { v } ^ { 2 }
$$

Applying the least squares regression method in the range of the reference speed points, adjusted road load coefficients $\mathrm { f _ { 0 , L } ^ { * } }$ and $\mathrm { f } _ { 2 , \mathrm { L } } ^ { * }$ shall be determined for $\mathrm { F _ { L } } ( \mathbf { v } )$ ; with the linear coefficient $\mathrm { f _ { l , L } ^ { * } }$ ; set to $\mathrm { f _ { 1 , H } }$ . The road load coefficients $\mathrm { f _ { 0 , i n d } , ~ f _ { 1 , i n d } }$ and $\mathrm { f } _ { 2 , \mathrm { i n d } }$ for an individual vehicle in the interpolation family shall be calculated using the following equations:

$$
\mathrm { f _ { 0 , i n d } = f _ { 0 , H } - \Delta f _ { 0 } \times \frac { \left( T M _ { H } \times R R _ { H } - T M _ { i n d } \times R R _ { i n d } \right) } { \left( T M _ { H } \times R R _ { H } - T M _ { L } \times R R _ { L } \right) } }
$$

or, if $( \mathrm { T M } _ { \mathrm { H } } \times \mathrm { R R } _ { \mathrm { H } } - \mathrm { T M } _ { \mathrm { L } } \times \mathrm { R R } _ { \mathrm { L } } ) = 0$ , the equation for $\mathrm { f _ { 0 , i n d } }$ below shall apply:

$$
\mathrm { f _ { 0 , i n d } = f _ { 0 , H } - \Delta f _ { 0 } }
$$

$$
\mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { l , i n d } } = \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { l , H } }
$$

$$
\mathrm { f _ { 2 , i n d } = f _ { 2 , H } - \Delta f _ { 2 } \frac { ( \Delta [ \mathrm { C _ { d } \times A _ { f } ] _ { L H } - \Delta \Delta [ \mathrm { C _ { d } \times A _ { f } ] _ { i n d } ) } } { ( \Delta [ \mathrm { C _ { d } \times A _ { f } ] _ { L H } ) } } } { } }
$$

or, if $\Delta ( \mathrm { C _ { d } } \times \mathrm { A _ { f } } ) \mathrm { L H } = 0$ , the equation for $\mathrm { F } _ { 2 , \mathrm { i n d } }$ below shall apply:

$$
\mathrm { f } _ { 2 , \mathrm { i n d } } = \mathrm { f } _ { 2 , \mathrm { H } } - \Delta \mathrm { f } _ { 2 }
$$

where:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \Delta \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { 0 } } = \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { 0 , H } } - \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { 0 , L } } ^ { \ast } } \\ & { } \\ & { \Delta \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { 2 } } = \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { 2 , H } } - \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { 2 , L } } ^ { \ast } } \end{array}
$$

In the case of a road load matrix family, the road load coefficients $\mathrm { f _ { 0 } }$ , f1 and $\mathrm { f } _ { 2 }$ for an individual vehicle shall be calculated according to the equations in paragraph 5.1.1. of Sub-Annex 4.

# 3.2.3.2.3. Calculation of cycle energy demand

The cycle energy demand of the applicable WLTC, $\mathrm { E _ { k } , }$ and the energy demand for all applicable cycle phases $\operatorname { E } _ { \mathrm { k } , \mathrm { p } }$ , shall be calculated according to the procedure in paragraph 5. of this Sub-Annex, for the following sets, $\mathbf { k } ,$ of road load coefficients and masses:

$\mathrm { k = 1 } ; ~ \mathrm { f _ { 0 } = f _ { 0 , L } ^ { \mathrm { * } } , ~ f _ { l } = f _ { l , H } , ~ f _ { 2 } = f _ { 2 , L } ^ { \mathrm { * } } , ~ m = T M _ { L } }$ (test vehicle L)   
${ \mathrm { k } } { = } 2 \mathrm { : } \mathrm { f } _ { 0 } = \mathrm { f } _ { 0 , \mathrm { H } } , \mathrm { f } _ { 1 } = \mathrm { f } _ { 1 , \mathrm { H } } , \mathrm { f } _ { 2 } = \mathrm { f } _ { 2 , \mathrm { H } } , \mathrm { m } = \mathrm { T M } _ { \mathrm { H } }$ (test vehicle H)   
$\mathrm { k = 3 ; ~ \Delta ~ f _ { 0 } = f _ { 0 , i n d } , ~ f _ { 1 } = f _ { 1 , H } , ~ f _ { 2 } = f _ { 2 , i n d } , ~ m = T M _ { i n d } }$ (an individual vehicle in the interpolation family)

These three sets of road loads may be derived from different road load families.

Calculation of the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ value for an individual vehicle within an interpolation family using the interpolation method

For each cycle phase p of the applicable cycle the mass of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions $\mathrm { { g } / \mathrm { { k m } , } }$ for an individual vehicle shall be calculated using the following equation:

$$
\mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O _ { 2 } - i n d , p } } = \mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O _ { 2 } - L , p } } + \left( \frac { \mathrm { E } _ { 3 , \mathrm { p } } - \mathrm { E } _ { 1 , \mathrm { p } } } { \mathrm { E } _ { 2 , \mathrm { p } } - \mathrm { E } _ { 1 , \mathrm { p } } } \right) \times \left( \mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O _ { 2 } - H , p } } - \mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O _ { 2 } - L , p } } \right)
$$

The mass of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions, $\mathrm { { g } / \mathrm { { k m } , } }$ over the complete cycle for an individual vehicle shall be calculated using the following equation:

$$
\mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O _ { 2 } - i n d } } = \mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O _ { 2 } - L } } + \left( \frac { \mathrm { E } _ { 3 } - \mathrm { E } _ { 1 } } { \mathrm { E } _ { 2 } - \mathrm { E } _ { 1 } } \right) \times \left( \mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O _ { 2 } - H } } - \mathbf { M } _ { \mathrm { C O _ { 2 } - L } } \right)
$$

The terms $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 , \mathrm { p } } , \mathrm { E } _ { 2 , \mathrm { p } }$ and $\mathrm { E } _ { 3 , \mathrm { p } }$ and $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { E } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { E } _ { 3 }$ respectively shall be calculated as specified in paragraph 3.2.3.2.3. of this SubAnnex.

3.2.3.2.5.

Calculation of the fuel consumption FC value for an individual vehicle within an interpolation family using the interpolation method

For each cycle phase p of the applicable cycle, the fuel consumption, $1 / 1 0 0 \mathrm { k m }$ , for an individual vehicle shall be calculated using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { F C _ { \mathrm { i n d , p } } = F C _ { L , p } + \left( \frac { E _ { 3 , p } - E _ { l , p } } { E _ { 2 , p } - E _ { l , p } } \right) \times ( F C _ { H , p } - F C _ { L , p } ) }
$$

The fuel consumption, $1 / 1 0 0 \mathrm { k m }$ , of the complete cycle for an individual vehicle shall be calculated using the following equation:

$$
{ \mathrm { F C } } _ { \mathrm { { i n d } } } = { \mathrm { F C } } _ { \mathrm { { L } } } + \left( { \frac { { \mathrm { E } } _ { 3 } - { \mathrm { E } } _ { 1 } } { { \mathrm { E } } _ { 2 } - { \mathrm { E } } _ { 1 } } } \right) \times \left( { \mathrm { F C } } _ { \mathrm { { H } } } - { \mathrm { F C } } _ { \mathrm { { L } } } \right)
$$

The terms $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 , \mathrm { p } } , \mathrm { E } _ { 2 , \mathrm { p } }$ and $\mathrm { E } _ { 3 , \mathrm { p } } ,$ and $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { E } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { E } _ { 3 }$ respectively shall be calculated as specified in paragraph 3.2.3.2.3. of this SubAnnex.

The individual $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ value determined in accordance with paragraph 3.2.3.2.4. of this Sub-Annex may be increased by the OEM. In such cases:

(a) The $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ phase values shall be increased by the ratio of the increased $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ value divided by the calculated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ value;

(b) The fuel consumption values shall be increased by the ratio of the increased $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ value divided by the calculated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ value.

This shall not compensate for technical elements that would effectively require a vehicle to be excluded from the interpolation family.

Fuel consumption and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ calculations for individual vehicles in a road load matrix family

The $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions and the fuel consumption for each individual vehicle in the road load matrix family shall be calculated according to the interpolation method outlined in paragraphs 3.2.3.2.3. to 3.2.3.2.5. inclusive of this Sub-Annex. Where applicable, references to vehicle L and/or H shall be replaced by references to vehicle $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ and/or $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ respectively.

3.2.4.1. Determination of fuel consumption and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions of vehicles $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$

The mass of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ emissions $\operatorname { M } _ { \mathrm { C O 2 } }$ of vehicles $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ shall be determined according to the calculations in paragraph 3.2.1. of this Sub-Annex for the individual cycle phases $\mathfrak { p }$ of the applicable WLTC and are referred to as $\mathrm { M } _ { \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } - \mathrm { L M } , \mathrm { p } }$ and $\mathrm { M } _ { \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } - \mathrm { H M } , \mathrm { p } }$ respectively. Fuel consumption for individual cycle phases of the applicable WLTC shall be determined according to paragraph 6. of this Sub-Annex and are referred to as $\mathrm { F C _ { L M , p } }$ and $\mathrm { F C _ { H M , p } }$ respectively.

3.2.4.1.1. Road load calculation for an individual vehicle The road load force shall be calculated according to the procedure described in paragraph 5.1. of Sub-Annex 4.

3.2.4.1.1.1. Mass of an individual vehicle

The test masses of vehicles $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ and $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ selected according to paragraph 4.2.1.4. of Sub-Annex 4 shall be used as input.

$\mathrm { T M } _ { \mathrm { i n d } } .$ , in kg, shall be the test mass of the individual vehicle according to the definition of test mass in paragraph 3.2.25. of this Annex.

If the same test mass is used for vehicles $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ , the value of $\mathrm { T M } _ { \mathrm { i n d } }$ shall be set to the mass of vehicle $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ for the road load matrix family method.

3.2.4.1.1.2. Rolling resistance of an individual vehicle

3.2.4.1.1.2.1. The rolling resistance coefficient (RRC) values for vehicle $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } } ,$ ${ \mathrm { R R } } _ { { \mathrm { L M } } } ,$ and vehicle $\operatorname { H } _ { \mathrm { M } } ,$ ${ \mathrm { R R } } _ { { \mathrm { H M } } }$ , selected under paragraph 4.2.1.4. of Sub-Annex 4 shall be used as input.

If the tyres on the front and rear axles of vehicle $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ or $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ have different RRC values, the weighted mean of the rolling resistances shall be calculated using the equation in paragraph 3.2.4.1.1.2.3. of this Sub-Annex.

3.2.4.1.1.2.2. For the tyres fitted to an individual vehicle, the value of the rolling resistance coefficient $\mathrm { R R } _ { \mathrm { i n d } }$ shall be set to the RRC value of the applicable tyre energy efficiency class in accordance with Table A4/2 of Sub-Annex 4.

In the case where individual vehicles may be supplied with a complete set of standard wheels and tyres and a complete set of snow tyres (marked with 3 Peaked Mountain and Snowflake – 3PMS) with or without wheels, the additional wheels/tyres shall not be considered as optional equipment.

If the tyres on the front and rear axles belong to different energy efficiency classes, the weighted mean shall be used, calculated with the equation in paragraph 3.2.4.1.1.2.3. of this Sub-Annex.

If the same rolling resistance is used for vehicles $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ , the value of $\mathrm { R R } _ { \mathrm { i n d } }$ shall be set to ${ \mathrm { R R } } _ { { \mathrm { H M } } }$ for the road load matrix family method.

3.2.4.1.1.2.3. Calculating the weighed mean of the rolling resistances

$$
\mathrm { R R _ { x } = ( R R _ { x , F A } \times \mathrm { m p _ { x , F A } ) + ( R R _ { x , R A } \times ( l - \mathrm { m p _ { x , F A } ) ) } } }
$$

where:

<table><tr><td>X</td><td>represents vehicle L,H or an indi- vidual vehicle;</td></tr><tr><td>RRLM,FA and RRHM,FA</td><td>are the actual RRCs of the front axle tyres on vehicles L and H respectively, kg/tonne;</td></tr><tr><td>RRind,FA</td><td>is the RRC value of the applicable tyreenergyefficiencyclassin accordance with Table A4/2of Sub-Annex 4 of the front axle tyreson the individual vehicle, kg/tonne;</td></tr><tr><td>RRLM,RA, and RRHM,RA</td><td>arethe actual rolling resistance coefficients of the rear axle tyres on vehicles L and H respectively, kg/tonne;</td></tr><tr><td>RRind,RA</td><td>is the RRC value of the applicable tyreenergyefficiency classin accordance with Table A4/2of Sub-Annex 4 of the rear axle tyres on the individual vehicle,kg/tonne;</td></tr><tr><td>mpx,FA</td><td>is the proportion of the vehicle mass in running order on the front axle.</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">RRx shall not be rounded or categorised to tre energy efficiency classes.</td></tr></table>

3.2.4.1.1.3. Frontal area of an individual vehicle

The frontal area for vehicle $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } } ,$ , $\mathbf { A } _ { \mathrm { f L M } } ,$ , and vehicle $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ , $\mathbf { A } _ { \mathrm { f H M } } .$ , selected under paragraph 4.2.1.4. of Sub-Annex 4 shall be used as input.

$\mathbf { A } _ { \mathrm { f , i n d } } , \mathbf { m } ^ { 2 }$ , shall be the frontal area of the individual vehicle.

If the same frontal area is used for vehicles $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } } .$ , the value of $\mathbf { A } _ { \mathrm { f , i n d } }$ shall be set to the frontal area of vehicle $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { M } }$ for the road load matrix family method.

# 3.3. PM

Calculation

PM shall be calculated using the following two equations:

$$
\mathrm { P M } = { \frac { ( \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { m i x } } + \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { e p } } ) \times \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { e } } } { \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { e p } } \times \mathrm { d } } }
$$

where exhaust gases are vented outside tunnel;

and:

$$
\mathrm { P M } = { \frac { \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { m i x } } \times \mathrm { P _ { e } } } { \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { e p } } \times \mathrm { d } } }
$$

where exhaust gases are returned to the tunnel;

where:

Vmix is the volume of diluted exhaust gases (see paragraph 2. of this Sub-Annex), under standard conditions;   
Vep is the volume of diluted exhaust gas flowing through the particulate sampling filter under standard conditions;   
$\mathrm { P _ { e } }$ is the mass of particulate matter collected by one or more sample filters, mg;   
d is the distance driven corresponding to the test cycle, km.

3.3.1.1.

Where correction for the background particulate mass from the dilution system has been used, this shall be determined in accordance with $\mathbf { \Delta } \mathbf { \succ } \mathbf { \underline { { M 3 } } }$ paragraph 2.1.3.1. of Sub-Annex $6 \rtimes$ . In this case, particulate mass $\mathrm { ( m g / k m ) }$ shall be calculated using the following equations:

$$
\mathrm { P M } = \left\{ \frac { \mathrm { P _ { e } } } { \mathrm { V _ { e p } } } - \left[ \frac { \mathrm { P _ { a } } } { \mathrm { V _ { a p } } } \times \left( 1 - \frac { 1 } { \mathrm { D F } } \right) \right] \right\} \times \frac { \left( \mathrm { V _ { m i x } } + \mathrm { V _ { e p } } \right) } { \mathrm { d } }
$$

in the case that the exhaust gases are vented outside the tunnel;

and:

$$
\mathrm { P M } = \left\{ \frac { \mathrm { P _ { e } } } { \mathrm { V _ { e p } } } - \left[ \frac { \mathrm { P _ { a } } } { \mathrm { V _ { a p } } } \times \left( 1 - \frac { 1 } { \mathrm { D F } } \right) \right] \right\} \times \frac { \left( \mathrm { V _ { m i x } } \right) } { \mathrm { d } }
$$

in the case that the exhaust gases are returned to the tunnel;

where:

$\mathrm { { V _ { a p } } }$ is the volume of tunnel air flowing through the background particulate filter under standard conditions;

$\mathrm { { P _ { a } } }$ is the particulate mass from the dilution air, or the dilution tunnel background air, as determined by the one of the methods described in $\mathbf { \Delta } \mathbf { \succ } \mathbf { \underline { { M 3 } } }$ paragraph 2.1.3.1. of SubAnnex $6 \rtimes$ ;

DF is the dilution factor determined in paragraph 3.2.1.1.1. of this Sub-Annex.

Where application of a background correction results in a negative result, it shall be considered to be zero $\mathrm { m g / k m }$ .

3.3.2.

Calculation of PM using the double dilution method

$$
\mathrm { V _ { e p } = V _ { s e t } - V _ { s s d } }
$$

where:

$\mathrm { V _ { e p } }$ is the volume of diluted exhaust gas flowing through the particulate sample filter under standard conditions;

$\mathrm { V _ { s e t } }$ is the volume of the double diluted exhaust gas passing through the particulate sampling filters under standard conditions;

$\mathrm { V _ { s s d } }$ is the volume of the secondary dilution air under standard conditions.

Where the secondary diluted sample gas for PM measurement is not returned to the tunnel, the CVS volume shall be calculated as in single dilution, i.e.:

$$
\mathrm { V _ { m i x } = V _ { m i x \ i n d i c a t e d } + V _ { e p } }
$$

where:

$\mathrm { \Delta V _ { m i x } }$ indicated is the measured volume of diluted exhaust gas in the dilution system following extraction of the particulate sample under standard conditions.

Determination of PN

PN shall be calculated using the following equation:

$$
\mathrm { P N } = \frac { \mathrm { V } \times \mathrm { k } \times \left( \overline { { \mathbb { C } _ { \mathrm { s } } } } \times \overline { { \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { r } } } } - \mathbb { C } _ { \mathrm { b } } \times \overline { { \mathrm { f } _ { \mathrm { r b } } } } \right) \times 1 0 ^ { 3 } } { \mathrm { d } }
$$

where:

PN is the particle number emission, particles per kilometre;

V is the volume of the diluted exhaust gas in litres per test (after primary dilution only in the case of double dilution) and corrected to standard conditions $( 2 7 3 , 1 5 \mathrm { ~ K ~ } ( 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and $^ { 1 0 1 , 3 2 5 \mathrm { ~ k P a } }$ ;

k is a calibration factor to correct the PNC measurements to the level of the reference instrument where this is not applied internally within the PNC. Where the calibration factor is applied internally within the PNC, the calibration factor shall be 1;
